summary: Plain C# finite state machine over IState, with optional condition-based transitions; you pump Tick() yourself.
problem: Behaviour written as an enum plus a switch plus a handful of bools stops being readable at about the third mode, mostly because there is nowhere to put the work that has to happen when a mode starts and ends. StateMachine gives each mode a class (see IState) and centralises the switching: SetState runs Exit on the old and Enter on the new, and the optional transition table turns 'if X then go to Y' into data you register once rather than branching scattered through Update. It is intentionally tiny and framework-free — no reflection, no attributes, no MonoBehaviour — so the whole flow is traceable by reading 50 lines.

workedExample.setup: StateMachineDemoRunner: two states whose Tick() accumulates Time.deltaTime into a public Timer that Enter() zeroes, with AddTransition(idle, active, () => idle.Timer >= 2f) and the mirror rule, running at a steady 60 fps (deltaTime = 1/60 s).
steps: Start() calls machine.SetState(idle). CurrentState was null so no Exit() runs; CurrentState becomes idle and idle.Enter() sets Timer = 0.

Each Update calls machine.Tick(), which runs CheckTransitions() FIRST and CurrentState.Tick() second. So on update frame N the condition is evaluated against the Timer value that frame N-1 left behind, namely (N-1)/60.
`idle.Timer >= 2f` first holds when (N-1)/60 >= 2, i.e. N - 1 >= 120, so the transition fires on frame 121. idle therefore ticked on frames 1 through 120 — exactly 120 ticks, 2.000 s.

On frame 121 SetState(active) calls idle.Exit(), assigns CurrentState = active and calls active.Enter() (Timer = 0); CheckTransitions then returns immediately. Tick() carries on and calls active.Tick(), so active already logs 1/60 s on the very frame it was entered, and idle.Tick() does not run on frame 121 at all.
Repeating the arithmetic for active: it ticks on frames 121..240, its condition first holds on frame 241, so the flip period is 241 - 121 = 120 frames = 2.000 s.
workedExample.result: Each state runs for exactly 120 Tick() calls (2.000 s at 60 fps) and the period does not drift, because Enter() re-zeroes the timer and the incoming state ticks on its own entry frame. The only asymmetry is the entry frame itself: a state's last Tick() is the frame before the switch, never the switch frame.

useCases: Enemy AI with Idle / Patrol / Chase / Attack modes, each owning its entry and exit work.
Racing or vehicle AI, as in RacingAIController, whose Racing / Recovering / Finished states are thin wrappers calling back into the controller.
Round or match flow — Lobby, Countdown, Playing, Results — where each phase swaps UI and input bindings.
Character locomotion modes (grounded, airborne, climbing) that need different physics settings applied on entry.
Driving a graph authored in the Visual State Machine editor: VisualStateMachineRunner builds exactly this class from the asset, mapping 'Any State' nodes to null-from transitions.

usage.codeNote: AddTransition is optional. Skip it entirely and call machine.SetState(...) from your own game logic if you would rather not use rule-based transitions — the source comment says as much.

apiNotes.CurrentState: The active IState, or null before the first SetState. Publicly readable, privately written. Tick() and SetState both use the null-conditional operator, so a machine with no state set is safe to pump.
apiNotes.SetState(IState): Returns immediately if newState is reference-equal to CurrentState; otherwise Exit() on the old state, assign, Enter() on the new. Because both calls are null-conditional, SetState(null) is a legal way to park the machine — it exits the current state and ticks nothing thereafter.
apiNotes.Tick(): The pump. Evaluates transitions and then ticks the current state, in that order. Call it once per frame from the owning MonoBehaviour's Update; nothing calls it for you, and there is no internal frame counter or delta.
apiNotes.AddTransition(IState, IState, Func<bool>: Appends a rule to an ordered list; there is no remove, clear, or duplicate check. A null 'from' means the rule is evaluated no matter which state is current (a global 'any state -> Dead'). CheckTransitions skips rules whose 'from' is neither null nor the current state, so conditions on irrelevant rules are not even invoked.
apiNotes.IsInState<T>(): Type test on the current state — returns true when the active state is a T. Use it for read-only queries (drive an animation, gate input); prefer a transition rule over branching on this.

gotchas.title: First match wins, and the check loop returns
gotchas.body: CheckTransitions walks the list in registration order and does `SetState(to); return;` on the first condition that is true — so registration order is priority order, and one rule at most fires per Tick. A broad any-state rule registered early shadows everything after it while its condition holds, which is usually exactly what you want for 'any state -> Dead' and exactly what you do not want for a permissive catch-all.

gotchas.title: A self-transition is refused rather than accepted
gotchas.body: A rule whose from and to were the same state wedged the machine: the check found it, called SetState, which returned immediately because that state was already current, and then returned out of the loop — blocking every later rule for as long as the condition held. AddTransition now rejects it with an error, and an any-state rule pointing at the current state is skipped rather than ending the scan.

gotchas.title: SetState cannot re-enter the current state
gotchas.body: The guard `if (CurrentState == newState) return;` means you cannot restart a state by re-selecting it — Enter() will not run again. It is a reference comparison, so it also means each state must be a single long-lived instance: `SetState(new IdleState(this))` in Update never matches, and fires Exit/Enter every frame.

gotchas.title: A state can be entered and exited without ever ticking
gotchas.body: Transitions are checked before the state body runs, so a condition that is already true on the next Tick takes you straight back out. Enter() and Exit() are guaranteed to pair up; Tick() running at least once is not guaranteed.

gotchas.title: Transitions can never be removed
gotchas.body: There is no RemoveTransition or Clear, and AddTransition does not dedupe. Re-running your setup method — on OnEnable, on a respawn, on a difficulty change — appends a whole second copy of every rule, and the duplicates keep evaluating forever. Build a fresh StateMachine instead of re-registering on an existing one.

gotchas.title: Nothing pumps it and nothing tears it down
gotchas.body: It is not a MonoBehaviour. If the owning component is disabled, Tick() stops being called and the machine freezes mid-state with no Exit(); if the owner is destroyed, Exit() is never called at all. Anything a state acquires and must release needs a matching release in the owner's OnDisable/OnDestroy.

gotchas.title: Conditions run every frame and exceptions escape
gotchas.body: Every rule whose 'from' matches the current state has its Func<bool> invoked on each Tick, before any state logic. Keep them cheap and side-effect free — a physics query or a GetComponent in a condition runs at full frame rate. An exception thrown inside one propagates straight out of machine.Tick() and takes the rest of your Update with it.
